name: Elobixibat
reviewed_by: William Gregory M. Rivero, MD, FPCP, DPSN
drafted_by: AI-assisted draft (Claude) for review by Dr. W. Rivero

overview.class: Ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT) inhibitor; laxative
overview.mechanism: Elobixibat blocks the ileal bile acid transporter, so more of the body's own bile acids reach the colon, where they increase colonic secretion and motility [[NAKAJIMA2018,KAMEI2020]]. It acts locally: plasma levels are in the picogram-per-milliliter range, protein binding exceeds 99%, and about 0.01% of a dose appears in urine [[PI]]. It also inhibits P-glycoprotein [[PI]].
uses: Chronic constipation, except constipation associated with organic diseases [[PI]]
The insert notes no clinical experience in drug-induced or disease-induced constipation [[PI]]
overview.uses_note: Indication from the Philippine package insert for Goofice (Hi-Eisai). Elobixibat has no US FDA or EU label. Statements are labeled by source: the insert, published studies, or clinical interpretation.

usual_adult_dose.dose: 10 mg (2 tablets) once daily before a meal; adjust to symptoms; maximum 15 mg (3 tablets) per day [[PI]]

dose_note: Dosing from the Philippine package insert. If abdominal pain or diarrhea occurs, reduce, interrupt or stop the drug, and reassess the need for continued treatment regularly rather than continuing it indefinitely [[PI]]. Regimens used in studies (for example, dosing before bedtime in the Thai hemodialysis trial) are study protocols, not prescribing advice [[JENAKSORNKUL2024]].
contraindications: Documented or suspected intestinal obstruction associated with a tumor or hernia (obstruction may worsen) [[PI]]
History of hypersensitivity to any ingredient [[PI]]

common: Abdominal pain (23.2%) and diarrhea (14.4%), the only reactions listed at 5% or more [[PI]]

1% to <5%: lower or upper abdominal pain, abdominal distension, nausea, abdominal discomfort, soft stools; abnormal liver tests (ALT, AST, gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase, LAP); dizziness; anemia; raised CK [[PI]]
In the phase 3 trials: abdominal pain 19% versus 2% with placebo and diarrhea 13% versus 0% over 2 weeks; 24% and 15% over 52 weeks, mostly mild [[NAKAJIMA2018]]
serious: Listed with frequency unknown: ischemic colitis, rectal bleeding [[PI]]
Swallowing a tablet still in its blister sheet can perforate the esophagus [[PI]]
No serious adverse events were reported in the small CKD and hemodialysis studies; this does not show that serious risks are absent [[JENAKSORNKUL2024,SHONO2024,MATSUYAMA2022]]

key_interactions.effect: Blood levels may rise and effects increase (P-glycoprotein inhibition; PH insert). With elobixibat 10 mg, dabigatran AUC was 1.17-fold (90% CI 1.00 to 1.36).
key_interactions.action: Use with care (PH insert). Digoxin and dabigatran accumulate in kidney failure; monitor accordingly.

key_interactions.effect: Blood level and effect may decrease (PH insert); AUC 0.78-fold (90% CI 0.73 to 0.83).

key_interactions.drug_or_class: Ursodeoxycholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid (bile acid preparations)
key_interactions.effect: Their effect may be reduced: elobixibat may block their reabsorption (PH insert).
May reduce elobixibat's effect by binding bile acids (PH insert).
May reduce elobixibat's effect by binding bile acids in the gut (PH insert).

monitoring: Stool frequency and form, abdominal pain and diarrhea; reduce, pause or stop if needed, and reassess continued use regularly [[PI]]

Clinical interpretation: low absorption does not remove the volume and electrolyte risk of diarrhea. In CKD and on dialysis, check volume status (interdialytic weight gain on hemodialysis), blood pressure and electrolytes if diarrhea develops
Digoxin or dabigatran co-therapy: exposure may rise [[PI]]
Counsel patients to take tablets out of the blister sheet before swallowing [[PI]]
Clinical interpretation: give bowel advice within the patient's fluid allowance; do not advise extra fluid for constipation without regard to dialysis fluid limits

hepatic: Use with care in serious liver disease; the drug may work less well with biliary obstruction or reduced bile acid secretion [[PI]]
Abnormal liver tests are listed adverse reactions (1% to <5%) [[PI]]
pediatric: Safety not established in low-birth-weight infants, neonates, infants or children; no clinical experience [[PI]]
older: Use with caution, for example at a reduced dose, because physiological function is generally reduced [[PI]]
pregnancy: Use only if the expected benefit outweighs the possible risk [[PI]]
Rat studies: maternal toxicity at 1,000 mg/kg/day and effects on offspring survival, growth and development at 350 mg/kg/day or more [[PI]]
breastfeeding: Avoid during breastfeeding; if treatment is essential, stop breastfeeding during treatment. In rats, radioactivity passed into milk [[PI]]
overdose: No overdose data; do not exceed the labeled dose and monitor the patient's response [[PI]]

evidence.title: Evidence in CKD, dialysis and chronic constipation
evidence.intro: The kidney-specific evidence is small, short and from Japan and Thailand. It supports better bowel function in CKD stages G3 to G5 and on hemodialysis. It does not show slower CKD progression, fewer cardiovascular events or deaths, lower uremic toxins, a phosphate- or potassium-lowering effect, or an advantage over other laxatives in dialysis.

rows.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; single center, Thailand. 46 hemodialysis patients (Rome IV), 43 analyzed.
rows.intervention: Elobixibat 10 mg/day or placebo, taken before bedtime (study protocol), 12 weeks.
rows.findings: Week 12 versus placebo: Bristol stool score +1.93 (95% CI 1.37 to 2.48); spontaneous bowel movements (SBM) +2.46/week (1.69 to 3.23); complete SBM +2.83/week (1.96 to 3.71 in the results text; the abstract gives 1.63 to 3.39); LDL cholesterol −12.41 mg/dL (−24.72 to −0.09; p = 0.048 in the text and figure, p < 0.001 in the abstract). p-Cresol not reduced (p = 0.46); phosphate and potassium changes not significant. No adverse events with elobixibat; no serious events.
rows.limitations: Small, single center, 12 weeks. Full-text figures shown where the abstract differs. 60% of placebo patients used rescue laxatives. Bedtime dosing differs from the label.

rows.design: Observational (retrospective efficacy review); single clinic, Japan. 54 hemodialysis patients already on elobixibat for at least 24 weeks.
rows.findings: SBM 2.0 ± 1.0 to 4.5 ± 2.2/week; Bristol score 1.7 to 3.8; satisfaction improved. Diarrhea 10/54 (18.5%), abdominal pain 2/54 (3.7%), all mild; no serious events. Serum phosphorus 5.12 to 4.40 mg/dL; potassium unchanged.
rows.limitations: No control group. Enrolling only patients who stayed on treatment at least 24 weeks selects those who responded and tolerated it. 83% also took other laxatives and 48% probiotics. Industry funded.

rows.design: Retrospective, single center, Japan. 42 patients: CKD G3 (6), G4 (9), G5 (9), G5D (18: 15 hemodialysis, 3 peritoneal dialysis).
rows.intervention: 5 mg (6 patients), 10 mg (29), 15 mg (7); half before and half after breakfast.
rows.findings: Stool frequency 0.5 to 1.1/day (1 week before versus 1 week after starting), regardless of dialysis, other laxatives or timing. At 4 weeks: LDL 90.9 to 77.5 mg/dL, HDL 44.9 to 57.0 mg/dL; phosphate, potassium and magnesium unchanged. Nausea and diarrhea in 2 patients; no serious events.
rows.limitations: Small, retrospective, uncontrolled; 20 of 42 on other laxatives; only 3 on peritoneal dialysis.

rows.design: Multicenter observational, Japan. 27 hemodialysis patients (Rome III) already on other constipation drugs.
rows.findings: SBM 2.6 ± 1.2 to 4.1 ± 2.1/week; Bristol score 1.9 to 3.6; total PAC-QOL score 1.83 to 1.17 (lower is better).
rows.limitations: No control group; add-on to other laxatives; 4 weeks.

rows.design: Retrospective cohort, Japanese hospital electronic records database. 11,062 patients started on elobixibat (2018 to 2022).
rows.findings: 78.7% stopped elobixibat within 360 days. Stage 5 CKD was among the factors associated with stopping.
rows.limitations: Database study: stopping is not the same as failure or intolerance. Authors include manufacturer staff.

rows.design: Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (132 analyzed) plus a 52-week open-label study (340); Japan; general chronic constipation.
rows.intervention: 10 mg before breakfast for 2 weeks; open-label 5 to 15 mg for 52 weeks.
rows.findings: Week 1 SBM increase from baseline 6.4 versus 1.7/week with placebo. Abdominal pain 19% versus 2%, diarrhea 13% versus 0%; over 52 weeks 24% and 15%, mostly mild.
rows.limitations: Not a kidney population; short randomized phase; long-term study uncontrolled; industry funded.

rows.design: Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, India. 150 randomized, 146 analyzed (modified intention to treat).
rows.findings: SBM change +3.83 versus +2.68/week; difference 1.15 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.99). Complete SBM response 49.3% versus 26.8%. Abdominal pain 7.9% versus 4.1%.
rows.limitations: Not a kidney population; 2 weeks; sponsor-run.

notes: The Japanese 2023 guideline recommends IBAT inhibitors for chronic constipation (strong recommendation, evidence level A). This is general constipation guidance, not a dialysis-specific grade [[IHARA2025]].

Magnesium-containing laxatives need care in impaired kidney function, with serum magnesium monitoring [[IHARA2025]]; the AGA–ACG guideline advises avoiding magnesium oxide in renal insufficiency because of hypermagnesemia [[CHANG2023]]. That guideline did not evaluate elobixibat; the omission is not a recommendation against it [[CHANG2023]].

Lipid and phosphorus changes in these studies do not establish cardiovascular benefit or a phosphate-lowering use, and phosphorus results differ between studies [[SHONO2024,MATSUYAMA2022,JENAKSORNKUL2024]].
Do not rank effect sizes across these trials: populations, endpoints and durations differ.

pk.bioavailability: Low systemic exposure (picograms per milliliter); with food, Cmax and AUC fall to about 20% to 30% of fasting values
pk.peak: About 2 hours (5 to 15 mg, before breakfast)
pk.metabolism: No plasma metabolites detected; in feces 96% unchanged and 3% monohydroxy form
pk.excretion_renal_pct: About 0.01% of a dose in urine (0.00% to 0.02% of a radiolabeled dose); about 103% of the radiolabel recovered in feces

draft_notes: Two kidney sources are not indexed in PubMed (Jenaksornkul 2024, Shono 2024); both were named for inclusion by Dr. Rivero (handoff, Nov 25 2026) and every figure used was checked against the full text.
The insert's midazolam interaction table calls the ratios 'greater', but both are below 1.0 (exposure decreased); the page reports the numbers.
Not cited: the ANMA/APAGE Chronic Constipation Consensus 2026 (J Neurogastroenterol Motil 2026;32:501-533) is confirmed on PubMed, but its elobixibat statements could not be opened for checking.

revision_log.change: Full monograph for an unlabeled drug: indication, dosing, contraindications, special populations, interactions and adverse reactions from the Philippine Goofice insert (verified section by section on the HI-Eisai professional site); evidence table and interpretation from PubMed-verified studies and guidelines, plus two non-indexed kidney studies at Dr. Rivero's direction; dose statements only from the insert.
